description: We are a team of academic researchers analyzing Earth's changing weather patterns, like true detectives.
summary:
EarthSignal is a free web map that tells you whether the environment in your district is really changing. It takes up to 25 years of NASA satellite and model data for 11 variables, including nitrogen dioxide, sulphur dioxide, fires, greenness and land temperature, and tests each of India’s 735 districts for a trend in every season. A trend counts only if it passes a Mann-Kendall test and survives a false-discovery-rate correction. Each one comes with its rate of change per decade and a 95% confidence interval. Of 134,399 tests, 12,741 looked significant but failed the correction, so they never reach the map.

Click a district to open its case file: what is rising, how fast, how certain the result is, and which factories and power plants sit nearby. The Policy tab ranks the confirmed problems in a state or district and drafts an AI brief that cites its sources, with every number checked against the data, so officials know where to act. A Learn view lets students work through guided cases and investigate their own area.

Officials, students and journalists ask about the place where they live, and they need to know which changes are real before acting on them.
details:
What it does
EarthSignal is a free web map that tells you whether the environment in your district is really changing. Pick a variable, such as nitrogen dioxide, sulphur dioxide, fires, greenness, land temperature or haze, and a season. Every one of India’s 735 districts is coloured by its trend: coral for rising, blue for falling, solid if the change is significant and faded if it is not.

Click a district to open its case file:

  • Verdict: change confirmed, false lead dismissed, or not proven.
  • Evidence: the rate of change per decade with a 95% confidence interval, a chart you can view yearly, monthly or with the seasons removed, and a CSV download.
  • Clues: every variable that changed significantly in that district.
  • Alibis: the apparent changes that failed the test.
  • Suspects: the factories and power plants nearby, shown as an association, not proof.

How it works
Python scripts pull up to 25 years of monthly NASA data, average it over each district boundary, and require at least 70% of months to be present, with no gap-filling. Whole-year trends use the seasonal Mann-Kendall test, and single seasons use the Hamed-Rao version, which corrects for autocorrelation. The size of each trend is Sen’s slope with a 95% confidence interval, and a t-test gives a second opinion. Because the tool runs 134,399 tests, it applies a Benjamini-Hochberg false-discovery-rate correction; 12,741 results that looked significant on their own fail it and never reach the map. We re-derived 28 series through NASA Giovanni, and 26 reached the same verdict. The two that disagreed compared model rainfall with satellite rainfall, so the app labels the model variables as not validated.

Benefits and intended impact
The Policy tab ranks the confirmed problems in a state or district and its surrounding airshed. An AI brief explains them, cites the facts it uses, and has every number checked by the page against the data, so officials can see where to act first. The Learn view gives students guided cases and an Investigate flow for their own area. Journalists and citizens get a plain answer about the place they live instead of a raw satellite grid.

Creativity
Most tools show data. EarthSignal gives a verdict and shows its working: false leads, uncertainty and the limits of each dataset sit beside every result. The detective framing of clues, alibis and suspects turns significance testing into something a non-scientist can follow.

Tools
Python (NumPy, pandas, xarray, GeoPandas, pymannkendall, statsmodels) for the data pipeline. Plain JavaScript and MapLibre GL for the map, with no build step. Vercel for hosting, with one serverless function calling Google Gemini for the brief. Claude helped write code and documentation. The code is open source under the MIT licence.

Factors we considered

  • Satellite cells are 25 to 100 km wide, so neighbouring districts can share one.
  • A trend is not a cause, and emission estimates are not measurements.
  • MODIS land temperature stops at 2022 because Terra’s orbit drifted afterwards.
  • Monthly fire counts are mostly zero, so fires are tested on yearly totals.
  • Model variables are flagged and kept out of policy rankings until validated.

The code is open source under the MIT licence: https://github.com/NamaiBest/Earth-Signal-Team_Friday
